opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that was one of the comparisons that really interested us when we were looking at inference costs. What we did was take a set of tasks, extractive question answering being one of them, and run them both through smaller models that were fine-tuned specifically for that task and through general-purpose generative models, the kind of instruction-tuned, sequence-to-sequence or decoder-only models people now reach for by default. We measured the energy consumed over the same number of queries, on the same hardware, so it was as apples-to-apples as we could make it.

What we found was pretty striking. For extractive QA, the task-specific models were dramatically more efficient. The difference was often an order of magnitude or more. And that makes sense when you think about what's happening under the hood. An extractive model is basically pointing at a span in the text: "the answer starts here and ends here." It's one forward pass, and it's a classification-style decision. A generative model is producing the answer token by token, so you're running the model over and over. On top of that, these models tend to have far more parameters, because they're built to do everything.

The other thing is that for a task like extractive QA, you often don't get much benefit in accuracy from using the big generative model. In some cases the specialized model does just as well or better, because it was trained precisely for that. So you're paying a big energy premium for flexibility you don't actually need.

That's really the takeaway I try to push: there's this trend of using one huge general-purpose model for everything, including tasks that are very well-defined and that we've had good, lightweight solutions for for years. If you know what your task is, whether it's extractive QA, classification, or sentiment analysis, it's worth asking whether you need a generative model at all. Because when you multiply those per-query differences by millions or billions of queries in deployment, the gap in energy, and in carbon emissions, becomes really significant.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that was actually one of the main findings of the study we did, "Power Hungry Processing," where we looked at a bunch of different tasks and a bunch of different models and measured the energy they consumed during inference. And the comparison between task-specific models and general-purpose generative models was really striking.

So for something like extractive question answering, you have models that were trained specifically to do that one thing. They take a context and a question, and they find the span of text in the context that answers the question. They're often pretty small, they're usually encoder-based, BERT-style architectures, and they're not generating anything. They're essentially just classifying where the answer starts and where it ends. So the amount of compute per query is tiny. We're talking about a fraction of a watt-hour for a thousand queries in some cases.

And then on the other side you have generative models, where you give them the same context and the same question, but they have to generate the answer token by token. Each token requires a forward pass through what is often a much bigger model, so the cost scales with both the size of the model and the length of what it produces. And when we actually measured it, we found that using a general-purpose generative model for extractive QA could be something like ten, twenty, up to thirty times more energy than using a task-specific model, depending on the size of the generative model. For some of the bigger ones the gap was even larger.

What I find interesting is that the task doesn't change. You're asking the same question and you want the same answer. But the architectural choice, generating versus extracting, completely changes the energy profile. And a lot of the time the task-specific model is just as accurate, or even more accurate, because it was fine-tuned on exactly that kind of data.

So the way I assess it is really on two axes. One is the raw energy per query, which we can measure directly with tools like CodeCarbon on the GPU. And the other is what I'd call the efficiency-to-utility ratio: are you actually getting anything out of that extra energy? And for a lot of these well-defined tasks, the honest answer is no. You're paying for generality you're not using. The generative model is a Swiss army knife, and sometimes you just need a screwdriver.

The reason it matters at scale is that these general-purpose models are being deployed everywhere now, including for things like search and QA where extractive approaches used to be the default. So that multiplier, ten, twenty, thirty times, gets applied to billions of queries a day. And nobody is really accounting for that, because inference costs are spread out and invisible, unlike training, where you have one big number you can point to.

r001.rationale: It says a general-purpose generative model used for extractive QA can consume up to 30 times more energy than a task-specific model for the same task.

astra-6.text:
The key is to compare them on the same task. If you have a question and a document containing the answer, an extractive model can identify the relevant passage, whereas a generative model produces an answer token by token. You can then measure how much energy each uses and whether that extra energy actually buys you a better answer.

There isn’t one fixed ratio—it depends on the model size, the hardware, and the length of the input and output. But generation can be much more energy intensive because you’re using a general-purpose system and repeatedly running computation to produce tokens for a task that a specialized model can handle more directly. So I’d ask: do you need generation here, or do you just need to find the answer in the text?

sol-6.1.text:
The key is to compare them on the same task. If you’re answering a question about a document, an extractive model finds the relevant passage and returns it. A generative model produces an answer token by token. That’s a different computational process, and it can use substantially more energy even when the result serves the same purpose.

So I’d measure the energy used across a set of questions, with comparable hardware and answer quality, and report energy per query. You also need to account for how long the inputs and outputs are, and distinguish the energy used to train the model from the energy used to run it.

The practical question is: do you need generation? If the answer is already in your document and you just need to retrieve it, a model trained for that task may meet your needs with much less computation.
